sections.h2: Where is the city of Frederick, Maryland?
sections.html:
Frederick is the seat of Frederick County, about 46 miles west of Baltimore, 50 miles north and slightly west of Washington, D.C., and 24 miles southeast of Hagerstown. It sits at 341 feet of elevation and covers 24.56 square miles, almost all of it land.

Daniel Dulany laid out the town by 1745, and it became the county seat when Frederick County was formed in 1748. Schifferstadt, built in 1756, is probably the oldest surviving house in the city. Frederick was a stop on the Great Wagon Road and the National Road, a rail and canal hub in the 1830s, and the site of the 1864 Battle of Monocacy.

The city counted 78,171 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate listed by Wikipedia is 92,059.

sections.h2: What is the layout of Frederick, and where are the older neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Frederick has a dense, walkable historic core surrounded by newer growth, and the core is where most of the preservation rules apply. Market, Patrick and East Streets carry more than 200 retailers, restaurants and antique shops in the Frederick Historic District, and downtown has about 600 businesses and organizations.

  • West Patrick Street follows the former National Road, now U.S. 40.
  • Monocacy Boulevard is a circular road that supports the core.
  • Culler Lake is a man-made lake downtown, and the church spires give the city its Clustered Spires nickname.
  • First Saturday draws about 11,000 people on average to downtown each month.

Wikipedia does not describe individual residential neighborhoods, so we do not name them here.

sections.h2: How do roads and transit shape the Frederick housing market?
sections.html:
Several major roads meet in Frederick: I-70, I-270, U.S. 15 and U.S. 340 meet here. I-70 runs east-west toward Baltimore and Hagerstown, I-270 runs southeast toward Washington, and U.S. 15 runs north toward Gettysburg.

Local TransIT buses and Greyhound also serve the city.

sections.h2: Who are the major employers in and around Frederick?
sections.html:
Fort Detrick is the largest employer in the Frederick area, with 10,827 employees in the 2025 figures reported by Wikipedia, and the county school board is next at 7,433. The list below shows the main public and institutional employers.

  • Frederick Health: 3,360
  • Frederick County Government: 2,810
  • Leidos Biomedical Research: 2,370
  • Frederick Community College: 1,369
  • City government: 977

Riverside Research Park, on the east side, hosts the National Cancer Institute's Frederick National Laboratory. Hood College and Frederick Community College are the city's higher education campuses, and Mount St. Mary's University has a campus in Frederick County.

sections.h2: What is the weather in Frederick, and what does it mean for a house?
sections.html:
Frederick has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and generally cool winters. The mean daily high is about 88.6 degrees in July and 43.1 degrees in January.

Average annual precipitation is 43.52 inches, and average snowfall is 16.5 inches. The state record high of 109 degrees was set in Frederick on July 10, 1936.

Flooding has a local history. The Carroll Creek flood control project began in the late 1970s to reduce flood risk to downtown from the 100-year floodplain. Its first phase, costing nearly $11 million, runs from Court Street to just past Carroll Street. The Carroll Creek Overlay District in the city code sets design standards for new construction and rehabilitation near the creek. The park along it includes brick paths, water features, pedestrian bridges and a 350-seat amphitheater, and Wikipedia reports more than $150 million in private investment underway or planned nearby, covering office, retail, residential and parking development.

sections.h2: What property tax rate applies inside the city of Frederick?
sections.html:
A house inside the city of Frederick had a combined real property rate of 1.7382 per $100 of assessed value in the fiscal 2025 state table, made of a county rate and a city rate. The table is published by the Department of Legislative Services from SDAT data.

Piece of the rate (fiscal 2025)Per $100 of assessed value
County rate in the city1.0077
Municipal rate0.7305
Combined1.7382
Unincorporated Frederick County, for comparison1.1100

The county's Treasury page says each municipality levies its own district tax for services like street maintenance, trash removal and police, and that homestead credit caps vary by municipality from 0 percent to 10 percent. We could not confirm from an official page whether the city portion appears on the county's bill, so ask the Treasury at 301-600-1111 before you pay.

sections.h2: What dates and appeal steps apply to a Frederick city owner?
sections.html:
Frederick County Treasury lists annual bills and the first installment as due September 30, with the second installment December 31, and interest of 1 percent per month starts October 1. Payments in July earn a 1 percent discount and August payments a one-half percent discount.

Assessments come from SDAT, which values property about every three years. An owner can appeal to the Supervisor of Assessments within 45 days of the notice date, to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days after that decision, and to the Maryland Tax Court within 30 days of the board's order. The SDAT office for the county is reached at 301-815-5350.

The county also lists a Senior Tax Credit of 20 percent of net county real property taxes for owners 65 or older who meet income limits, and a Homestead Tax Credit that limits yearly increases on a principal residence.

sections.h2: What historic district and code rules affect a Frederick seller?
sections.html:
In the city of Frederick, exterior work on a designated site or a property in a Historic Preservation Overlay district needs a certificate of approval from the Historic Preservation Commission. The commission reviews exterior features only and does not consider interior layout.

  • Changes do not have to be visible from the street to need review. Routine maintenance and landscaping with no material effect are exempt.
  • The commission has 45 days to act on a complete application, and silence means approval unless the applicant agrees to more time.
  • A certificate expires after three years without a building or zoning permit, with one six-month extension available.
  • Decisions can be challenged in the Circuit Court for Frederick County within 30 days.

Properties outside the overlay can still face demolition review when a plan removes more than 25 percent of floor area, changes significant roof lines or moves the structure.

For rental condition, the county says complaints about properties inside the city go to city inspectors at 301-600-3825.

faqs.q: What is the property tax rate in Frederick, MD?
faqs.a: The fiscal 2025 state table shows 1.7382 per $100 of assessed value inside the city, made up of a 1.0077 county rate and a 0.7305 municipal rate. Rates are reset each year, so check the current notice.

faqs.q: When is Frederick property tax due?
faqs.a: September 30 for annual bills and the first installment, and December 31 for the second installment. Interest starts October 1 at 1 percent per month, and a 1 percent discount applies to July payments.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Frederick property tax?
faqs.a: Call the Frederick County Treasury at 301-600-1111 for billing, and SDAT at 301-815-5350 for the assessed value. The Treasury is at 30 North Market Street, open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.

faqs.q: Does the Frederick Historic Preservation Commission review a house sale?
faqs.a: No, a sale itself does not require approval. Exterior work on a designated or overlay property does, and the commission has 45 days to act on a complete application.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Frederick house with back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, unpaid tax can be paid from the closing proceeds by the title company. Ask the Treasury for a lien certificate or tax status report to see the exact amount before you set the closing date.
